title: Hydrogen-Rich Water Alleviates Drought-Induced Oxidative Stress and Maintains Leaf K⁺/Na⁺ Homeostasis in Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.)
content: Drought stress is a major constraint on cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) production in arid regions. Hydrogen-rich water (HRW) has been reported to mitigate abiotic stress, but its field-level effects on antioxidant dynamics, ion homeostasis, and yield formation remain poorly documented. A field experiment was conducted in Aksu, southern Xinjiang, China, with three treatments: rain-fed control without spray (A), tap-water irrigation with purified-water foliar spray (B), and HRW irrigation (May–June) combined with HRW foliar spray (September) (C). Leaf samples were collected at 0, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h after spraying for antioxidant enzyme activities, malondialdehyde (MDA), proline, H2O2, and chlorophyll, and at 0, 12, and 24 h for water-soluble Na+ and K+. HRW treatment markedly increased peroxidase (POD) activity at 6–12 h (peak 3363.3 U g-1 FW at 12 h; P < 0.05 vs. A) and maintained a numerically higher leaf K+/Na+ ratio at 12 h (3.71) compared with A (3.42) and B (2.46). Although Na+ accumulated at 24 h in all treatments, C maintained the highest absolute K+ concentration (12.27 g kg-1 DW). These physiological improvements were associated with a higher boll number per plant (60.2 vs. 21.4 in A), higher seed cotton yield per plant (138.0 vs. 70.0 g), and a higher lint yield per plant (70.0 vs. 34.7 g). HVI analysis showed that fiber length and uniformity in C were numerically higher than in A, while breaking strength remained comparable, indicating that the yield gain did not compromise fiber quality. Our results suggest that HRW alleviates drought stress in cotton by enhancing antioxidant defense and preserving K+ homeostasis during the boll-setting stage, thereby improving boll retention and lint yield. However, because the spray carrier differed between treatments, the specific contribution of dissolved H2 cannot be fully isolated in this design.
